instances.brief: The queue drain is in progress. Your job is to resume message producers at the right moment — once queue depth falls below 1,000 messages. Resume too soon and the backlog regrows; wait too long and orders pile up unnecessarily.
instances.teaches: Resuming producers at a stable low-depth threshold avoids oscillation. Acting on CPU or publish-rate during a drain is a common mistake — those metrics stay high by design while the backlog clears.

given.rule: Resume producers when queue depth falls below 1,000 messages.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Queue depth was still at 4,200 msgs when you clicked. Producers flood back in and the backlog regrows past 6,000 within a minute — the drain stalls.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Resuming before depth falls below 1,000 reintroduces load faster than the drain can absorb it.

wrong_outcomes.shows: You waited 20 s past the threshold. Producers were held offline unnecessarily and 1,400 orders sat queued longer than required.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Holding producers off after the threshold is clear wastes capacity and extends customer-facing delays.

wrong_outcomes.shows: You acted on a gauge other than queue depth. Consumer CPU sits above 85% for the whole drain by design and publish rate is near zero while producers are paused, so neither says when it is safe — queue depth fell below 1,000 unnoticed and producers stayed offline another 40 s, delaying 1,400 orders.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Consumer CPU stays high while the queue drains by design. The triggering condition is queue depth, not CPU.

instances.reveal: Queue depth falls linearly as consumers drain at full speed. Consumer CPU stays elevated during the drain because consumers are working hard — that is correct, not a problem. Publish rate is zero because producers are paused. The only signal that the system is ready to resume producers is queue depth crossing below 1,000 messages.

instances.brief: You are tuning an alerting rule for {{node_name}}. Watch the gauges and act at the moment the rule's condition becomes true — that is the point your alert must match.
instances.teaches: Alert thresholds should match the metric's actual crossing point, not an earlier wobble. Acting on a transient peak below 250 ms reproduces the noisy false-page the team was trying to eliminate.

given.rule: The tuned alert should fire when p95 latency stays above 250 ms — act when p95 crosses 250 ms.

wrong_outcomes.shows: p95 was at 238 ms when you clicked — a sinusoidal wobble, not a sustained crossing. The old alert used this same threshold and produced 3–5 false pages per day.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Clicking on a transient peak below the threshold copies the false-positive pattern the team wanted to fix.

wrong_outcomes.shows: You waited until t=25 s. p95 was 290 ms by then — 40 ms above the threshold for 7 s before you acted. The alert fires late and the on-call engineer misses the early window.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: The rule must fire at the crossing, not after the metric has climbed well past it.

wrong_outcomes.shows: You acted on a gauge other than p95 latency. Error rate was still 0.6% and request rate was flat when p95 crossed 250 ms and kept climbing to 320 ms — the tuned alert is keyed to latency, so on the real incident it would never fire.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Error rate is a lagging indicator here. The rule targets p95 latency, which crosses first.

instances.reveal: p95 latency rises steadily with a sinusoidal wobble of ±12 ms. The wobble causes brief peaks near 240–245 ms before the true crossing at roughly 18 s. Error rate and RPS are decoys — they are rising but neither crosses the threshold the rule specifies. The correct approach is to watch p95 specifically and click at the moment it passes 250 ms.

instances.brief: You are configuring {{node_name}}'s autoscaler. Watch the gauges and act at the moment the policy's trigger fires — that is where scale-out should begin.
instances.teaches: Autoscaler thresholds must match CPU specifically, even when p95 latency moves first. p95 rises before CPU crosses 70% because existing instances saturate, but the correct trigger for adding capacity is CPU, not latency.

given.rule: Policy: scale out when average CPU crosses 70%.

wrong_outcomes.shows: CPU was at 61% when you clicked — still well below 70%. The autoscaler fires prematurely and adds instances while the cluster still has headroom, wasting 60 credits.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Firing the scale-out before CPU crosses 70% over-provisions the cluster and inflates cost.

wrong_outcomes.shows: You clicked at t=22 s when CPU had been above 70% for 7 s. p95 reached 210 ms during the delay — the scale-out happened too late to prevent latency impact.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Waiting beyond the window means the cluster has been running overloaded while the new instance spins up.

wrong_outcomes.shows: You acted on a gauge other than CPU. Memory holds near 62% and p95 rises with load, but the autoscaler policy reads average CPU — no scale-out fires, and CPU keeps climbing past 90% while the cluster stays at its current size.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: The policy specifies CPU as the trigger. p95 is a symptom of high CPU, not the signal the autoscaler watches.

instances.reveal: CPU rises steadily from 48% at 1.6% per second, with a ±3% oscillation on a 5-second period. It crosses 70% at roughly 14.65 s. Memory stays flat at 62% — it is a decoy. p95 latency starts climbing earlier because the existing instances saturate before CPU hits the threshold, but the policy says to act on CPU. Click CPU at the 70% crossing to fire the autoscaler at the right moment.
